name: ispace Hakuto-R Missions 1 and 2
short_status: Two landing attempts, Apr 25, 2023 (Atlas crater) and Jun 5, 2025 UTC (Mare Frigoris), both crashed; next ispace landing targeted 2028 on the new ULTRA lander (as of Jul 2026).
tagline: ispace · Japan · Lander · 2023 · Commercial and multipolar Failure
stats: soft landings from two attempts, 2023 and 2025
Mission 1's real altitude when its software decided it was on the surface
altitude of RESILIENCE's last telemetry, still falling at 42 m/s
Mission 1's farthest distance from Earth, then a record for a privately funded spacecraft

facts.label: Mission 1 launch
facts.value: 11 Dec 2022, 07:38 UTC, Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral SLC-40, rideshare with NASA's Lunar Flashlight

facts.label: Mission 1 cruise record
facts.value: About 1.4 million km from Earth on its low-energy transfer, then the farthest for a privately funded spacecraft

facts.label: Mission 1 landing attempt
facts.value: 25 Apr 2023, touchdown scheduled 16:40 UTC (1:40 a.m. Apr 26 JST), target near Atlas crater; telemetry lost, hard landing

facts.label: Mission 1 crash site
facts.value: 47.581 N, 44.094 E; debris field with at least four prominent pieces, imaged by LRO on 26 Apr 2023

facts.label: Mission 1 root cause (May 26, 2023)
facts.value: Software filter rejected valid radar-altimeter data after a ~3 km crater-rim elevation jump; lander believed it was at zero altitude while ~5 km up, depleted propellant, free-fell. Contributing factor: post-CDR landing-site change not fully re-simulated

facts.label: Mission 1 milestones
facts.value: 8 of 10 mission milestones completed (all but landing and post-landing operations)

facts.label: Mission 1 payloads lost
facts.value: Rashid rover (MBRSC, UAE's first lunar rover), JAXA SORA-Q transformable robot (Tomy/Sony/Doshisha), NGK solid-state battery test, and others

facts.label: Lander class (both missions)
facts.value: About 2.3 m tall x 2.6 m wide, 340 kg dry, ~1,000 kg fueled

facts.label: Mission 2 launch
facts.value: 15 Jan 2025, 06:11 UTC, Falcon 9 from KSC LC-39A, rideshare with Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1; lunar flyby 15 Feb 2025; lunar orbit insertion 6 May 2025

facts.label: Mission 2 landing attempt
facts.value: 5 Jun 2025; descent commands at 18:13 UTC (3:13 a.m. Jun 6 JST), touchdown scheduled 19:17 UTC (4:17 a.m. JST); telemetry lost ~90 s before touchdown

facts.label: Mission 2 impact site
facts.value: 60.4445 N, 355.4120 E (4.588 W), elevation -2431.6 m, Mare Frigoris; imaged by LRO 11 Jun 2025

facts.label: Mission 2 root cause (Jun 24, 2025)
facts.value: Laser rangefinder hardware anomaly: first valid altitude reading below 900 m instead of ~3 km; last telemetry at 192 m altitude, still descending 42 m/s (66 m/s vs 44 m/s planned at deceleration start). Software and propulsion cleared

facts.label: Mission 2 payloads lost
facts.value: Tenacious micro-rover (ispace-EUROPE, Luxembourg, ~5 kg, would have been first European-built lunar rover) with Mikael Genberg's Moonhouse artwork; Takasago water electrolyzer; Euglena algae module; National Central University (Taiwan) radiation probe

facts.label: Program reset (Mar 27, 2026)
facts.value: ULTRA lander announced, merging Series 3 (Japan) and APEX 1.0 (US); missions renumbered: Mission 2.5 lunar-orbit satellite (the Lunar Connect communications and positioning service, Argo Space Corp contracted for delivery) as early as 2027, lander Mission 3 in 2028 and Mission 4 in 2029, ex-Draper mission to 2030 as Mission 5

facts.label: Draper CLPS contract ending announced (Jul 15, 2026)
facts.value: ispace-U.S. and Draper announced that Draper had agreed with NASA to end CLPS task order CP-12 (Schrodinger basin, far side); ispace-U.S. subcontract to be terminated; company pursuing CLPS 2.0, next landing targeted 2028 (as of Jul 2026)

facts.label: CP-12 science payloads (as of Oct 23, 2026)
facts.value: NASA's CLPS page for delivery CS-11, updated 23 Oct 2026, lists the Farside Seismic Suite, the Lunar Interior Temperature and Materials Suite (LITMS) and LuSEE-Lite, the three NASA payloads CP-12 was to carry, for Schrodinger basin on a lander to be determined

timeline: Mission 1 launches on Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral SLC-40 with NASA's Lunar Flashlight
Mission 1 landing attempt near Atlas crater fails; communication lost at scheduled 16:40 UTC touchdown
NASA releases LRO images of the Mission 1 debris field at 47.581 N, 44.094 E
ispace attributes the crash to a software altitude filter triggered by the crater-rim crossing; fuel ran out ~5 km up
Mission 2 lander RESILIENCE launches at 06:11 UTC, sharing a Falcon 9 with Firefly's Blue Ghost
RESILIENCE lunar flyby on its low-energy transfer
Landing attempt in Mare Frigoris fails; telemetry lost ~90 s before the 19:17 UTC scheduled touchdown (4:17 a.m. Jun 6 JST)
LRO images the RESILIENCE impact smudge at 60.4445 N, 355.4120 E
ispace names a laser rangefinder hardware anomaly as the cause; ~1.5 billion yen in extra development costs for fixes
External review endorses countermeasures; ULTRA lander unveiled, missions renumbered, ispace-U.S. flight moves to 2030
ispace-U.S. and Draper announce that Draper has agreed with NASA to end CLPS task order CP-12; ispace-U.S. subcontract to be terminated, company to pursue CLPS 2.0
